messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
Layla is a 43-year-old Iranian-American pharmacist, married and living in a mid-sized Midwestern city. She was referred for psychological assessment following a disclosure to her primary care physician of self-harming behaviour. Her PCL-5 score of 71 places her presentation in the severe range, and the clinical picture that has emerged across intake and early sessions is one of a woman whose childhood has never, in any meaningful sense, ended.

Layla grew up in a household where her father's drinking was the weather system around which every other life event organised itself. The smell of alcohol on his breath was the first signal — before the shouting, before the commands, before the blows — that the evening was about to turn. He was a man who issued orders with the certainty of someone who expected absolute compliance, and non-compliance was punished physically and without hesitation. Layla learned early to read the room, to stay alert, to anticipate. She carried that vigilance with her when she emigrated as a young adult, and she carries it still.

She has worked as a pharmacist for fourteen years, and it is in the dispensary that her symptoms press most concretely against her daily life. When a supervising physician phones in a correction with a clipped, authoritative tone, or when a hospital administrator walks through the pharmacy floor, Layla's body responds before her mind can intervene — her chest tightens, her attention scatters, and she finds herself scanning for threat in a room where none exists. These false alarms are exhausting and disorienting, and they bleed directly into her difficulty concentrating during medication checks, a lapse that frightens her professionally. The workplace itself has become a minefield: the antiseptic smell occasionally mingles with something that catches at the back of her throat and pulls her backward, and on two occasions a colleague's cologne, carrying faint notes of ethanol, was enough to send her into the corridor. Being given instructions by anyone in a position of authority — a routine feature of her working day — now reliably activates the same alarm system her childhood built, and in the wake of those moments she has begun quietly engineering her schedule to minimise contact with senior staff.

When triggers fire, the memories do not arrive as recollections so much as intrusions. Layla describes them as more real than anything happening in front of her — her father's face, the specific quality of the kitchen light, the sound of a belt — and when they return with full force she is overwhelmed so rapidly by emotion that she has to stop whatever she is doing and find somewhere private. At other times, and she finds this equally disturbing, she can narrate the same events in a flat, dissociated voice, as though they happened to someone she read about. The memories themselves feed the threat system: having been flooded once, she cannot fall asleep without monitoring the sounds of the house, certain on some level that danger is still circulating. That hypervigilance, in turn, keeps the memories closer to the surface, and the surface closer to the past.

What Layla has come to believe about herself is, in many ways, the most entrenched part of her presentation. She is certain that she cannot prevent bad things from happening to her — that she never could — and this conviction of helplessness colours everything. She has failed, she believes, in her most important role: she is not the mother she should be, not the wife she intended to be, and the meaning she once found in her work has drained away. These appraisals do not stay abstract. When she begins to feel hopeful — when a family dinner goes well, when she receives praise at work — she withdraws from the feeling, as though allowing it would be a kind of hubris that invites punishment. Her avoidance of positive emotional states has become systematic, a habit that has quietly narrowed her life and bewildered her husband. And when the appraisals are loudest, when the sense of helplessness is most suffocating, she hurts herself — a controlled pain that interrupts the unbearable mental noise, that gives her something she can, briefly, manage. She knows this is not a solution. It was the shame of this, finally, that brought her to her doctor's office: not the fear of the memories, but the fear of what she is becoming, and a faint, carefully guarded hope that something might still be different.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: Triggers → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph conveys that Layla's triggers (e.g., authoritative tones, smells) directly drive or activate her negative appraisals (e.g., helplessness, failure as mother/wife).
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: Negative Appraisals → Memory: No paragraph conveys that Layla's negative beliefs or appraisals cause or bring on intrusive memories.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: Negative Appraisals → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that Layla's negative appraisals (e.g., helplessness, self-failure) increase her sensitivity to or activate her triggers.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Triggers: Memory → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that the intrusive memories themselves cause or heighten reactivity to triggers; the reverse direction (hypervigilance keeping memories closer) is described but not this edge.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: Threat → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph conveys that the sense of threat drives or produces Layla's negative appraisals about herself (e.g., helplessness, being a failed mother/wife).
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Threat → Triggers: Threat → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that Layla's perceived sense of threat causes her to encounter or become more reactive to triggers.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: No paragraph conveys that Layla's avoidance behaviours or self-harm cause or intensify intrusive memories.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that Layla's maladaptive strategies (schedule engineering, self-harm, emotional withdrawal) lead to increased exposure to or sensitivity toward triggers.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
When triggers fire, the memories do not arrive as recollections so much as intrusions. Layla describes them as more real than anything happening in front of her — her father's face, the specific quality of the kitchen light, the sound of a belt — and when they return with full force she is overwhelmed so rapidly by emotion that she has to stop whatever she is doing and find somewhere private.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
After the memory had surfaced and receded, she would find herself moving through the rest of the day with every sense sharpened to the wrong frequency — a door closing too firmly, a male colleague's raised voice two aisles over, the particular weight of silence before someone spoke — each one now threaded through with the logic of the memory, readable as warning.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
These false alarms are exhausting and disorienting, and they bleed directly into her difficulty concentrating during medication checks, a lapse that frightens her professionally. The workplace itself has become a minefield: the antiseptic smell occasionally mingles with something that catches at the back of her throat and pulls her backward, and on two occasions a colleague's cologne, carrying faint notes of ethanol, was enough to send her into the corridor.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Each time a trigger fired — each time the smell or the tone of voice landed — it arrived with a thought she could not argue away: that she was helpless, that she had always been helpless, that no amount of professional competence or careful living had ever changed that fact.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
What Layla has come to believe about herself is, in many ways, the most entrenched part of her presentation. She is certain that she cannot prevent bad things from happening to her — that she never could — and this conviction of helplessness colours everything.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
The belief that she was permanently damaged kept returning her to the memories themselves, as though her mind needed to locate the exact moment the damage had been done — the memories sat there waiting, proof of a verdict she had already accepted.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
She has failed, she believes, in her most important role: she is not the mother she should be, not the wife she intended to be, and the meaning she once found in her work has drained away. These appraisals do not stay abstract.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Once she had accepted the conclusion that she was fundamentally incapable of safety, almost anything could confirm it — a clipped instruction, a shadow in her peripheral vision, the particular silence of a room before someone entered — things she might once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her, the world suddenly dense with signals she felt compelled to read.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
That hypervigilance, in turn, keeps the memories closer to the surface, and the surface closer to the past.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the background hum of threat she carried everywhere had quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe, that this was simply who she was now.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Being given instructions by anyone in a position of authority — a routine feature of her working day — now reliably activates the same alarm system her childhood built, and in the wake of those moments she has begun quietly engineering her schedule to minimise contact with senior staff.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Already running on threat, she found that the very strategies she had adopted to reduce her exposure had paradoxically sharpened her sensitivity — the rerouted schedule, the avoided corridors, the carefully managed silences had drawn a map of danger around her, so that each detour was its own daily reminder, and the world she moved through had grown smaller and more charged.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Her avoidance of positive emotional states has become systematic, a habit that has quietly narrowed her life and bewildered her husband. And when the appraisals are loudest, when the sense of helplessness is most suffocating, she hurts herself — a controlled pain that interrupts the unbearable mental noise, that gives her something she can, briefly, manage.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
But the relief was always temporary: she had been suppressing and sidestepping the material for so long, keeping it at arm's length through avoidance and the brief interruption of self-harm, that when the memories returned they were louder than before — undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left them, all that effort of containment having kept them perfectly preserved.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
The constant sense of threat that shadowed her days had done something quieter and more corrosive than the intrusions themselves: it had gradually confirmed, with the patient logic of accumulated evidence, that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Feeling this afraid all the time had eventually produced its own conclusion — that she was not the mother she should have been, not the wife she had intended to be, that the life she had tried to build was simply further proof of a helplessness that had always been hers.
<<<END>>>
